After spending years trying to engage in rational debate with these people I came to the realization that it's essentially pointless. You can't discuss anything in an honest way with them because their minds are already made up. Everything is filtered through their framework of idealism. This results in an absurd perspective where they disregard something not because they disagree with the premise, but because the premise disagrees with their beliefs. Logic/empiricism/science/evidence/statistics don't matter. "Multiculturalism=good" is a law of nature. "All races are equal" is a law of nature. Anything that contradicts these laws must therefore be dismissed. "Multiculturalism can't be bad because multiculturalism is good" is a perfectly logical statement in their minds, no matter how obviously fallacious it is. That is their objective truth, so any argument you put forward is immediately invalid because it violates that truth.

On a related note, I remember listening to a debate between Jared Taylor and Tim Wise in which Wise said something like "the white race is an invalid concept because there are IQ/achievement differences between groups within the white race." So basically because we're not all the same that apparently means we shouldn't identify as white but rather as specifically Irish, Russian, Polish, etc. (never mind the fact that it's people like him who have fueled white nationalism by lumping us all together as beneficiaries of undue privilege and perpetrators of mass injustice). My point here is that he pretty much acknowledges the existence of the exact thing he was arguing against—that there are fundamental differences between different groups of people. I honestly think they know this to be true (there's a reason they choose to live in white neighborhoods and send their kids to white schools). I think their rejection of the evidence is simply a coping mechanism to reduce their cognitive dissonance. According to Leon Festinger, who proposed the theory, there are four ways to accomplish this:

  1. Change behavior or cognition
  2. Justify behavior or cognition by changing the conflicting cognition
  3. Justify behavior or cognition by adding new cognitions
  4. Ignore or deny any information that conflicts with existing beliefs

Here are a relevant few paragraphs from his writings:

It is also possible to add a new cognitive element which, in a sense, "reconciles" two elements that are dissonant. Let us consider an example from the literature to illustrate this. Spiro gives an account of certain aspects of the belief system of the Ifaluk, a nonliterate society. The relevant points for our purposes here are as follows:

  1. In this culture there is a firm belief that people are good. This belief is not only that they should be good but that they are good.

  2. For one reason or another, young children in this culture go through a period of particularly strong overt aggression, hostility, and destructiveness.

It seems clear that the belief about the nature of people is dissonant with the knowledge of the behavior of children in this culture. It would have been possible to reduce the dissonance in any number of ways. They might have changed their belief about the nature of people or have modified it so that people are wholly good only at maturity. Or they might have changed their ideas about what is and what is not "good" so that overt aggression in young children would be considered good. Actually, the manner of reducing dissonance was different. A third belief was added which effectively reduced dissonance by "reconciliation." Specifically, they also believe in the existence of malevolent ghosts which enter into persons and cause them to do bad things.

As a result of this third belief, the knowledge of the aggressive behavior of children is no longer dissonant with the belief that people are good. It is not the children who behave aggressively—it's the malevolent ghosts. Psychologically, this is a highly satisfactory means of reducing the dissonance, as one might expect when such beliefs are institutionalized at a cultural level. Unsatisfactory solutions would not be as successful in becoming widely accepted.

I think the correlation between this example and our current situation is pretty clear.
Cognitive dissonance and the mind of an anti-racist

I don't think these things are mutually exclusive. The majority of SJWs are simply indoctrinated into their beliefs, not part of the system carrying out the indoctrination. When all the evidence goes against what they believe new explanations must be created to satisfy their dissonance, e.g. white privilege. I do suspect that the rationalizations are provided to them rather than created internally, but the result is the same—they can continue believing in their fairy tale society.

This should work. You can make it stick through reboots by taking the command you come up with, saving it in a file and setting it to run on login. Your file should look like this:

#!/bin/bash
 xrandr --output VGA-0 --mode 1440x900 --primary --right-of DP-3 \
 --output DP-3 --mode 1600x900

Naturally, you should substitute in whatever your xrandr command is.

You will need to mark the resulting file executable, either by right clicking it, selecting properties, and allowing execution under the permissions tab, or by running chmod +x filename.sh in the commandline. Also, by convention, the file extension should be .sh.
